1:
The heading is examined before the message. Gill says the word means a prophecy, as the Targum has it, not what the prophet dreamed but what he saw. Ellicott sets it among the three recognised headings of prophetic books, word, burden and vision, all used in a general way with no intention of distinguishing kinds of prophecy; Nahum combines burden and vision. It is therefore unnecessary, he says, to suppose the future was unfolded as a succession of pictures spread out before the mind, since vision here means revelation, however supplied. Calvin reads the preface as a disclaimer: the prophet brought nothing human but declared what was presented to him from above, making God the author so the doctrine should not be suspected, for what faith can be put in men except as they are ruled by the Spirit of God.

Ellicott finds a difficulty in the second half of the heading. After the words announcing who speaks concerning Edom we should expect the message itself, not the statement that a message had come; of the explanations offered he calls two most plausible, that the twofold heading is due to a later hand, or that the added words merely state that the seer was divinely inspired. Which is right, he says, must be settled by the view taken of the authorship.

Who the prophet was nobody claims to know. Keil and Delitzsch says nothing certain can be established, since the heading gives only the name, meaning servant of Jehovah, and does not even name his father; tradition variously identifies him with a governor of the palace under Ahab, with a captain sent against Elisha, or with an Edomite proselyte. Clarke says the questions of who he was and when he prophesied have been asked from the remotest antiquity and have received no answer worthy of recording.

The rumour is taken as an order. Calvin explains that the word is properly a hearing, and that although some understand it of what was taught, it probably refers to the tumultuous rumours which commonly precede wars. His point is that wars are not stirred up at random: when a tumult arises its beginning is not from the earth, for God himself is the mover. Henry calls it a rumour, or rather an order, from the Lord of hosts, a decree which can neither be reversed nor resisted, with a herald sent to alarm the nations; when God has bloody work to do among the enemies of his church, he adds, he will find out both hands and hearts to do it. Wesley says the report comes from God first and from Nebuchadnezzar after. Ellicott finds a suggestiveness in the vagueness of the summons, since the nations, without distinction of good or bad, become instruments of the chastisement of pride.

How small Edom was is measured two ways. Ellicott makes it a mere speck on the map beside the giant empires, and gives the original Mount Seir, which this prophet calls Mount Esau, as a tract about a hundred miles long and nowhere more than twenty broad. Gill reports the same from Aben Ezra, but prefers with Kimchi to read the past for the future after the prophetic manner, so that the meaning is I will make thee small; Keil and Delitzsch reaches the same result by saying the perfect describes a resolution whose fulfilment is as certain as if it had occurred, and Clarke observes that God ever attributes to himself the rise and fall of nations. Calvin inclines instead to read the clause as a reproof rather than a threat, that the Idumeans grew arrogant while confined to the narrow passes of mountains, since it is less bearable when a man is elated with pride whose condition is not honourable; and he grants that the reading he declines has been adopted nearly by the consent of all.
3:
What the pride rested on is listed first. Gill names their wealth and riches, amassed by robbery, their military skill and courage, their friends and allies, and above all their fortresses both natural and artificial, which persuaded them that no enemy could come at them. Wesley adds the character that went with the country, that the Edomites were, as most mountaineers are, a rough hardy and daring people, and proud above measure, and that the deceiving lay in magnifying their strength above what it really was.

Where exactly they lived is a question of one word. Clarke reports from Jerome that the whole southern part of Palestine, from Eleutheropolis to Petra and Aialath, was full of caverns hewn out of the rocks, the people having subterranean dwellings like ovens; and he notes that some take the Hebrew word for rock as the name of Petra, the capital. Calvin canvasses the renderings, that some read between the windings of the rock, that the same words are given elsewhere as the encirclings of the rock, and that Parkhurst makes them the cracks or fissures; he allows that the word may allude to the name of a city, but objects that clefts do not comport with a city situated on a plain within ranges of mountains, and so takes it of Mount Seir. Keil and Delitzsch approaches the same word from its root, which is not used in Hebrew, and notes that where it occurs elsewhere it stands in parallel with a term that points to the sense of a refuge or asylum, a meaning since confirmed by others.

Calvin makes the verse a piece of derision. The prophet laughs the Idumeans to scorn, he says, because they relied on their fortresses and thought themselves, according to the common saying, beyond the reach of darts, and on that account insulted the Israelites and despised God himself. He allows that there was not wanting a reason why they should be insolent, since the country really was well fortified; but he holds that all they promised themselves were mere delusions, because God cared nothing for their fortresses and counted them as nothing. The general lesson he draws is that it is the greatest madness for men to rely on their own power and despise God, who could dissipate by a single blast every idea of defence that is in us.

Keil and Delitzsch reads the following verse as the demonstration that the reliance was worthless, and explains its construction: the object does not arrive until the second clause, so that the sense is, if thou makest thy nest high like the eagle, which builds upon the loftiest jagged rocks; and the thought is then hyperbolically intensified, if thy nest were set among the stars. He notes that an older oracle stands behind the wording. Gill takes the same figure more simply, of a bird that soars aloft and flies out of sight, higher than any other, or else reads the clause as exalting the habitation to the height of an eagle's nest.

That the height is no defence at all is where they converge. Clarke says that though like this bird you should get into the highest cliff of the highest rock it will not avail, since when Jehovah has determined a people's destruction their deepest caves and their highest rocks are equally useless. Wesley makes the contest unequal in a different way: God who is in the heavens would throw them down, and when men could not marshal armies against them the stars should fight in their courses against them, for nothing can stand which God will cast down. Calvin puts the same conclusion as a challenge, asking whence this security comes that they think enemies can do them no harm, and answering that it comes only from delusions, since the Lord says he will bring them down from wherever they have climbed.
5:
The two comparisons are read the same way by all. Clarke states them plainly: if thieves entered the dwellings they would not have taken everything, and if grape-gatherers entered the vineyards some gleanings would have been left, whereas the Chaldeans stripped the country bare; and the prophet speaks as if the desolation had already taken place. Keil and Delitzsch makes that the point of the construction, that the prophet sees the overthrow as already done and supposes two cases of plundering in which something is nevertheless left, so as to exhibit the more vividly the complete clearing out of Edom. Calvin adds that the enemy would not be like night robbers who take what comes to hand, but would leave the houses wholly empty. He also says why the point was pressed, to mitigate the grief of the faithful, who thought themselves miserable in being plundered alone while their neighbours dwelt safe and even shared the spoil.

The searching out of the hidden things is where the mountains stop helping. Gill says that although they hid in caves and dens, their enemies found them there and plucked them out, and Wesley that all they had laid up in the most secret places is seized by soldiers. Calvin explains why this was worth exclaiming at. Even when a country is plundered, conquerors dare not enter places of danger, and when there are narrow passes they avoid them, supposing some ambush is laid there; but Edom's rocks were almost inaccessible and full of conveniences for concealing wealth, so the prophet speaks with astonishment. The lesson he draws is that as men seek hiding places for themselves in vain, so in vain do they conceal their riches, since the hand of God penetrates beyond sea, land and the lowest deep. Ellicott adds that the word for the hidden things comes from a verb meaning to hide, and that whether treasures or hiding-places are meant cannot be determined, since it occurs nowhere else in the language.

How the allies failed them is disputed. Ellicott takes the most natural explanation to be that fugitives from the ruin of Edom, fleeing into allied territory for help, are basely driven back to their frontier and left to their fate; the desertion, he adds, is put forward as the due retribution on Edom for treachery towards his natural ally, his brother Jacob. Keil and Delitzsch rejects that reading outright, on the ground that the suffix cannot refer to the few fugitives who escaped the massacre but applies to Edom as a nation, so that the ambassadors sent to seek help, and in their persons the Edomites themselves, are sent back to the frontier. Gill canvasses several possibilities, that the allies received the ambassadors kindly and escorted them to the borders but never stood to their engagements, or, as Kimchi has it, followed them to the border when they were carried captive as if lamenting while assisting the enemy. Clarke names the Chaldeans as the confederates, whose agents the Idumeans had become.

Calvin makes the desertion a lesson about confidence. It is in God's power to change the minds of men, so that friends are suddenly inflamed with rage, and there was no need to send far for instruments of vengeance. He then turns it against the policy itself: had Edom stayed quiet in its clefts it would have fared better, whereas it ran to Assyria and Chaldea, and that was the cause of its ruin.

The wound in the last clause is another disputed word. Ellicott notes that it occurs elsewhere in the sense of a festering wound, that the older translators render it ambush or snare, and that moderns prefer net; Clarke and Wesley keep the snare, Wesley making it one armed with sharp points. Clarke adds that plans were all in operation against Edom while it was too infatuated to see its danger.
8:
What the destroying of the wise men means is settled with care. Keil and Delitzsch denies that it means the wise men will all be slain, or slain before any others, and holds that they are destroyed as wise men by the withdrawal of their wisdom; the second clause, which names only discernment, and the parallel passages elsewhere both support this. Gill gives the practical effect, that there would be no counsellors at court to advise what should be done, whether because they were taken off by death or because their wisdom was turned into folly. Clarke notes that the Edomites were remarkable for wisdom and prudence, which is what makes the threat pointed.

Calvin makes the verse a warning about the conceit of wisdom. Though men are in many respects blind whom God does not guide by his Spirit, the worst blindness, he says, is to be inebriated with a false conceit of understanding; when a man thinks he can perceive whatever is needful and cannot be circumvented, his wisdom is insanity, and it would be better to be an idiot than drunk in that way. He observes that God permits the ungodly to felicitate themselves long on their own acumen, and points to the Venetians of his own day, whom nobody can persuade that consummate wisdom exists anywhere but among themselves, and to kings who ascribe their standing to their own foresight. The point he draws from the wording is that it was no wonder the Idumeans had until then been wary and taken the best counsel, since it was not the Lord's purpose to deprive them of wisdom before the time of vengeance came; and the warning he adds is that those who excel in understanding must not abuse a singular gift, as the ungodly do who turn their wisdom into cunning.

What Teman stands for is not agreed. Gill takes it as one part of the country of Edom, named from a son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau, a district famous for men of might, who would now be so dispirited that instead of defending their country they would throw away their arms and run away in a fright. Clarke calls it one of the strongest places in Idumea, put here for Idumea itself, and glosses the mount of Esau as Mount Seir; Wesley says it was a principal city. Calvin reports that some think a particular country is meant, since the word means the south with regard to Judea, but judges it more probable that Idumea is addressed, since Teman was a grandson of Esau and a part of Arabia bore the name, so that a part is taken for the whole.

Calvin then draws the two halves of the sentence together. The courage and strength of men, he says, are in the hand of God no less than their understanding, so that as he dissipates whatever wisdom is in them, he also enervates and breaks down their hearts until they come to nothing of themselves. Were those proud of their strength to consider this rightly they would learn at last to submit in true humility; but the world cannot be made to believe it, though God shows here as in a picture that men, however they flourish for a time, would vanish were he not sustaining them, and that what seems understanding and strength in them is empty smoke.

The last word of the verse has been moved by some critics. Calvin reports that certain of them remove the term for slaughter to the beginning of the next verse, but sees no sufficient reason for it; the word itself, he adds, means a slaughter in which no one remains alive. Keil and Delitzsch reads it to the same effect, that the heroes despair in order that every one may be cut off from the mountains of Esau.
10:
Why this one charge carries the whole sentence is Henry's starting point. Having read a doom of utter ruin, he says, it is natural to ask what evil Edom has done; many things were amiss, but the single crime that filled their measure is the injury done to the people of God. The violence is aggravated twice over: once because it was done to a brother, to whom one ought to be a redeemer; and again because that brother was in covenant with God, who takes what is done against him as done against himself, so that whoever touches Jacob touches the apple of the eye of Jacob's God. That, Henry concludes, makes it high treason.

The naming of the brother is weighed by the others. Gill lists the aggravations, that Jacob was an honest plain-hearted man whom the Lord loved, his own and only brother; but he understands the charge of the posterity of the one against the other, and not of the destruction of Jerusalem only but of the grudge shown on every occasion. Ellicott suggests the birth-name Jacob is used purposely to bring out the full wickedness of the descendants of Esau, and draws a contrast: Israel long maintained a friendly feeling towards the kindred race as a religious duty, whereas Edom from the first was jealous and hostile, never imitating the generous disposition of its own great ancestor. Clarke says we need not look for particular instances, since Esau was not more inimical to Jacob than the Edomites uniformly were to the Jews, and adds that they even urged the Chaldeans, when Jerusalem was taken, to level the temple with the ground.

Calvin turns the same word against their standing. He says the brother is named not for honour's sake but to set out the cruelty more fully, since consanguinity did nothing to keep them from raging against their own bowels; they were descended from Abraham and from Isaac and had the symbol of circumcision. From the threat of being cut off for ever he draws a further conclusion, that the punishment would not be temporary as in the case of Israel, whom God chastises within limits because he never forgets his covenant, but such as proved the Idumeans aliens; their claim to circumcision counted for nothing, since they had impiously profaned it.

What standing on the other side amounted to is then pressed. Gill takes it as standing aloof to watch the ruin with pleasure, when as brethren they should have helped against the common enemy, or else as going over and joining the enemy. Wesley reads it as setting themselves in battle array against their brother; Clarke says they not only failed to help when they might, but assisted his foes and came in for a share of the booty. Ellicott catches a different shade, that Edom acted the part of an enemy instead of a friend though probably in the base character of a neutral, ready to take the winning side.

Calvin answers the excuse he expects them to make, that they were not the cause of the ruin and that what necessity compelled should not be counted a crime. The prophet dissipates the plea with a question, were you not there; it was no wonder that a distant people shed the blood of Judah, but you, of the same blood, whom neighbourhood obliged either to help or at least to condole, were as one of the enemy. Even unarmed, he adds, taking pleasure in so mournful a spectacle was the worst oppression of all.

Ellicott finds it hard to choose between forces and substance in the second clause, and sets the three clauses as a climax, the plunder of the open country, entry into the gates, and the casting of lots in the capital. Keil and Delitzsch renders the warnings that follow as plain prohibitions rather than reproaches.
12:
How these clauses are to be read is settled first. Gill notes that some render them in the imperative, do not look, and so with the clauses that follow. Calvin agrees that the prophet speaks by way of prohibition, and calls it a personification in which God teaches the Idumeans the duties of human kindness; but he adds that these ought to have been engraven on their hearts already, since in forgetting humanity they had departed from everything nature requires, so that the prophet is reminding rather than instructing them.

The looking is not a matter of the eyes only. Calvin observes that the verb is used in Scripture of men who lie in wait, or anxiously desire something, or rejoice at what they witness, and takes it here for delight in the misery of the chosen people. Clarke turns it into a rule: it shows a malevolent heart to rejoice in the miseries even of those who have acted unkindly towards us, and if God punishes a man for treating us cruelly and we rejoice at it, we make his crime our own, so that as we have done it shall be done to us. Wesley says they looked with joy on the affliction.

The day their brother became a stranger is explained as the exile. Calvin approves of those who take the alienation for banishment, adding the reason they leave out, that such a change came over the people that they put on a new appearance, every favour being withdrawn until the very look of the nation was deformed.

Entering the gate is treated as the aggravation. Gill takes it of the gates of Jerusalem, into which the Edomites came with the Chaldeans; Calvin supposes they made an irruption with the invaders when they ought to have stayed at home and lamented the slaughter of their brethren. He sets a rule of ordinary feeling against them: if I cannot save my friend from death I shall at least withdraw, and if made to look on without being able to help I would rather close my eyes, for the tenderest sympathy is in the eyes. That they entered the city willingly with the enemy showed them no better than wild beasts; and they were not content to let their brethren be pillaged but became robbers themselves.

The place where they waited is disputed. Gill offers a spot where two or more roads meet, so as to stop the fugitives whichever way they took, or else a breach in the walls, which is how Wesley takes it, a gap by which some might have escaped. Calvin traces the word to a root meaning to break, allows that some make it a place where one road is cut into two, says he is pleased with that but will not confine the word to it, and prefers the idea of a going forth. He dismisses another proposal, that the sense is they should not have stood still but should have reached out a helping hand, as too frigid and strained. His own observation is more telling: the Assyrians and Chaldeans, coming from far, would not have known the country and would have feared being entrapped, whereas the Idumeans, acquainted with all the roads, could post themselves at every outlet, so that flight, the only safety left, was cut off by the one people who knew where it led.

The last clause completes the account. Clarke says they stood in the passes to prevent escape, throwing the fugitives back into the teeth of their enemies, and had gone so far as to deliver up the few who had taken refuge among them; Wesley names the Chaldeans as those to whom the survivors were handed over. Keil and Delitzsch observes that the warning is supported by what follows, a day in which Edom and all the enemies of Israel receive just retribution.
15:
Why the sentence widens to all the nations is explained two ways by Calvin. He allows that the prophet may be reasoning from the greater to the less, so that if God will not spare other nations Edom cannot escape his hand; on that view the Idumeans deserved a double vengeance, since compared with them the fault of the Assyrians and Chaldeans looks small, those being aliens and professed enemies who could plead some cause for the war, while the Idumeans were neighbours and kindred. But he offers a simpler reading as well, that God would take vengeance not on one nation or two but on all, showing himself the judge of the whole earth, from which it follows that the Idumeans must render an account with the rest.

The verse also answers an inference they had drawn. Calvin observes that when the Idumeans saw the kingdoms of Israel and Judah trodden under foot they concluded that the children of Abraham were being punished for despising their own prophets and for their perverseness, and so exempted themselves and everyone else; the prophet answers that God had indeed been the judge of his own people but is judge of the whole world too. Clarke states the same correction more sharply, that God will not associate Edom with himself in the judgments he inflicts, since Edom is guilty too and will have its punishment in due course along with the other sinful nations.

How near the day was is taken up by both. Gill understands the time to be fixed by the Lord for punishing all the heathen round about, the Egyptians, Philistines, Ammonites and Moabites among them, and says the clause is set down for Edom's sake, to show that they could not expect to escape in the general ruin; he places the destruction about five years after the fall of Jerusalem, so that it might truly be called near, and infers that the prophet spoke within that space. Calvin makes the nearness a matter of God's own reckoning, since the Lord does not hasten after the manner of men but knows his own seasons, and it is ever accomplished that when the ungodly think themselves at rest, sudden destruction overtakes them. Wesley says only that the time was appointed for punishing this and other nations, and that the measure returns on Edom for having dealt perfidiously and ravenously with Jacob.

Who did the drinking on the holy mountain is disputed. Clarke takes the address to be to the Jews, so that as they had been visited and punished upon the holy mountain in Jerusalem, other nations should be punished in their own countries; Wesley reads it the same way, that as God's own people had drunk deep of the cup of affliction, so other nations should much more, until they utterly perished. Calvin takes the drinking in the opposite sense, of the triumphs and rejoicings of the Idumeans, a part being put for the whole: as they had rejoiced on the holy mountain, so all the nations should drink in their turn. He finds in it a further proof of their greed, since they had taken a share of the spoil along with the foreigners; and he makes the second drinking different from the first, so that the nations shall consume all their substance, those who enriched themselves with the spoils of their brethren and feasted on the holy mountain becoming in the end the food of others. Gill notes that the Targum applies the words to the Edomites.

Keil and Delitzsch marks the turn the prophecy now takes, from the judgment upon all the heathen to the completion of the kingdom of God by the raising up of Israel, with Mount Zion standing as an asylum for those who are delivered while judgment falls on the nations around.
17:
The first word of the promise is read as a company, not an act. Ellicott prefers the marginal sense, the fugitives of Israel who survived the recent calamity, supporting it from passages where the term stands in parallel with remnant; while judgment falls on the nations, Mount Zion becomes an asylum for the Israelites who had been scattered. Keil and Delitzsch says the same, that on the mountain the Edomites desecrated by their drinking carousals there will be the multitude preserved throughout the judgment. Gill notes the alternative rendering, they that escape, and reads the deliverance as fulfilled by Cyrus, by the Maccabees, and at last by the Messiah.

Calvin explains why the promise was needed at all. The Jews might have objected that it was nothing to them if the Lord avenged their wrongs while they were being destroyed; and the answer is that the escape is promised not from Mount Zion but in the very mountain, so that God would restore those who seemed already lost. From this he draws the rule that the punishment by which the Lord chastises his people is ever for a time, and that whenever he wounds his church the remedy is prepared with the wound.

The holiness is taken both as a state and as a guarantee. Keil and Delitzsch makes the mountain a sanctuary and so inviolable, which the heathen will no longer dare to defile, and infers that the rescued crowd upon it will be a holy people. Calvin makes the word a sign that God would be mindful of his covenant, since he is said to have profaned the land when he gave it into the hands of enemies. Henry turns it into an order of grace, that where there is salvation there shall be sanctification in order to it, since wherever God designs glory he gives grace; holiness is itself a great deliverance. Clarke reads it historically, that they would separate from their idols and become a better people than before the captivity.

Whose possessions are meant is disputed. Ellicott asks whether they are Israel's own possessions that had been lost or those of the nations, notes that the Vulgate, following the old Greek, read the words as those who had possessed them and so found here the subjugation of the heathen tribes, and judges the parallelism to favour the other view. Henry holds that these promises, however fulfilled in the return from Babylon, have their full accomplishment in the salvation wrought by Christ.

Who the two houses are is not agreed. Gill allows that Jacob may denote Judah and Benjamin and Joseph the ten tribes, but thinks they may signify one and the same, since all the tribes will be united at the time meant. Ellicott takes the opposite line, that although in the previous verse the house of Jacob seems to embrace all restored Israel, here, set opposite the house of Joseph, it must be Judah; Keil and Delitzsch agrees.

Calvin answers a second doubt with the figure of the fire. The Idumeans were flourishing while Israel and Judah went into exile, which might have driven the exiles to despair; but though the house of Jacob seemed dead, a fire would be kindled to consume Edom. What he finds remarkable is the manner of it: the vengeance came while the Jews were in exile and could not move a finger, so that its cause did not appear to the Idumeans at all, and we must look to the purpose of God, who meant by this example to show how much he loved his church. Clarke gives the outward history, that after the return the Jews broke out as a flame upon the Idumeans and reduced them to slavery, and observes that the promise of none remaining means the end of a nation, not of every individual; Wesley names the same fulfilment but looks for a fuller.
19:
The geography is read as expansion on every side. Clarke sets the four points out plainly, Edom to the south, the Philistines to the west, Ephraim to the north and Gilead to the east, so that those who returned from Babylon were to extend themselves everywhere; he notes that Alexander the Great gave Samaria to the Jews and that Hyrcanus subdued the same country. Keil and Delitzsch states the principle, that after the destruction of its foes the nation of God takes their land and extends its territory on every side. Gill and Wesley keep the plain sense, that the Jews of the south would seize Idumea next to them and those of the plain the country of the Philistines, with their own ancient inheritance.

Calvin sets the promise against the original grant. God had promised the posterity of Abraham the whole land from the Euphrates to the sea, and that land was never possessed by them, through their own sloth and ingratitude; David enlarged the borders but only made tributary those whom God had commanded to be destroyed, so that the blessing was never fulfilled, the people themselves putting the hindrance in the way. The prophet now promises the returning exiles a full inheritance. But Calvin then says openly that this prophecy too has never been completed, since only a small portion of the land was ever held; and from that he concludes that the passage speaks of the kingdom of Christ, under whom the church was restored and the borders enlarged, so that the Jews recovered not merely their former condition but a kingdom of greater splendour.

Zarephath is identified from the geographers. Gill takes the clause of the land formerly held by the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, which belonged to Zidon and was called Sarepta of Sidon; he notes that Pliny mentions it as a place where glass was made, and suggests the name may come from the melting of metals; that Josephus places it between Sidon and Tyre; and that Elijah dwelt there, a little tower being shown as his habitation in the time of Jerom. Clarke agrees that Phoenicia as a whole is meant.

Sepharad nobody has placed. Clarke calls it a difficult word and lists the guesses, the Bosphorus, Spain, France, the Euphrates and a district in Chaldea, adding that one writer made it a part of Edom; Wesley settles for a region of Chaldea. Calvin admits the obscurity and reports that some take Canaan here for the Illyrians and Germans and the Gauls, and Zarephath for Spain, asserting it as though it were plain from history; he declines these glosses, and concludes that the prophet means all the territories once promised to the children of Abraham, so that the people should recover not only what they had lost but what had never been given them to hold.

Who the saviours are is the last question. Gill reports that some take them of Zerubbabel and Joshua, who restored the civil and church state after the captivity, or of Judas Maccabeus and his brethren, called saviours as the judges of old were; but he prefers to understand the apostles and the ministers of the word, called saviours because they publish salvation, while Christ remains the only Saviour. Clarke allows both, and reports that several manuscripts read instead the preserved, those delivered from the captivity; he adds that since the Asmonean princes joined the priesthood to the state, that may be what is meant by the kingdom being the Lord's. Calvin takes the plural as an allusion to the history of the judges, when the people were so distressed that their deliverance was almost incredible and yet was given so as to show the hand of God; and he argues from it that the Messiah cannot be a redeemer of the common class, since saviours are ranked under him as his ministers.
